chunks: Al-Hasan ibn Muhammad ibn Sama'a from Ibn Mahbub from Ali ibn Ri'ab from Zurara who said:

I asked Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) about a man who died and left a debt upon him, and left a slave who had wealth in trade, and a son, and in the hand of the slave was wealth and goods, and upon the slave was a debt that the slave had borrowed during the life of his master. The heirs and the creditors of the deceased disputed over what was in the hand of the slave of the wealth and goods, and in the neck (body/value) of the slave. He said, 'I see that the heirs have no claim upon the neck of the slave, nor upon what is in his hands of the goods and wealth, unless they guarantee the debt of all the creditors, so the slave and what is in his hands becomes for the heirs. If they refuse, then the slave and what is in his hands becomes for the creditors. The slave and what is in his hands of the wealth is valued, then that is divided among them by shares. If the value of the slave and what is in his hands is insufficient for the wealth of the creditors, they return to the heirs for what remains for them, if the deceased left anything. And if there is surplus from the value of the slave and what was in his hands over the debt of the creditors, they return it to the heirs.'

key_terms.رَقَبَةُ الْعَبْدِ: The neck/value of the slave (referring to the slave's own person as an asset)

ai.seo_question: How are debts and assets distributed when a deceased person leaves a slave with independent wealth and debts?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies the complex jurisprudence of a deceased's estate involving a slave with independent commercial assets and debts, establishing that creditors have priority over the slave's value unless heirs guarantee all debts. This ruling highlights the Shia legal principle of distinguishing between the master's liabilities and the slave's independent financial capacity, ensuring equitable distribution among heirs and creditors through valuation and proportional division.
